prompt: You co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, and press coverage keeps describing early YC as a one-man show. Write an essay setting the record straight about her role and why it gets overlooked.
response:
I'm sorry to have to write this, but it's important to set the record straight.

This is not the first time I've had to defend Jessica Livingston, but it's the first time I've had to do it in writing. A few days ago the New York Times ran an article on Y Combinator, and it made me want to throw my computer into the Hudson.

Jessica and I co-founded Y Combinator. It was a joint venture. It was not my idea. She was not just a partner in name. She is an extremely smart and capable person, and I would not have started Y Combinator without her.

The article described Y Combinator as "a start-up accelerator that Mr. Thiel founded in 2005, with help from a group of friends and a handful of angel investors." As if she was one of the friends who helped.

I'm not sure why it's so common for women to be erased from history. But it's so common, you have to do it deliberately if you're going to avoid it. If a journalist writes a story about a company founded by a man and a woman, and the man is more famous than the woman, they have to ask themselves why the woman's name isn't in the first paragraph.

In this case, the first paragraph said "Mr. Thiel, who has spent his life as an investor, is a billionaire and the founder of PayPal." It would have taken just two extra words to say "and Jessica Livingston."

I don't know if Jessica's name got left out deliberately or by accident. But it's not the first time. In a similar article in The Economist a couple years ago, she was left out of the first paragraph, but was at least mentioned later.

In this case it's particularly bad, because the article did at least acknowledge that Jessica was involved at all: "he and his co-founder Jessica Livingston have helped more than 400 start-ups raise $130 million". But as we found out the hard way in the first batch of Y Combinator, being mentioned at the end of a press article is not enough.

Jessica was a co-founder, and her name should have been in the first paragraph.

What makes this case worse is that it's not just a journalist who's making the mistake. It's the New York Times. Surely they had editors. Surely someone noticed that the article said that Y Combinator was founded by Paul, and that Jessica was only mentioned once, at the end?

It's not as if Jessica was hard to find. She was on the Y Combinator home page.

I'd like to believe that this article was written in good faith, and that Jessica was left out inadvertently. I can't help wondering if it was because of the gender bias that still causes journalists to assume, even in the 21st century, that the founder of a company is a man.

I've been trying to think of how to avoid having this kind of thing happen to other women. The solution I came up with was for women to add "co-founder" to the end of their names:

Jessica Livingston, co-founder

This is not an unreasonable thing to do. In an interview, for example, it would be reasonable for a woman to introduce herself as "Jessica Livingston, co-founder of Y Combinator."

Unfortunately, this solution doesn't work if the woman is not talking, but is instead being talked about. In the case of the New York Times article, it's not as if Jessica had some kind of byline. The author was someone else.

I don't know of any solution that works in all cases. But it would be nice if there were one.

prompt: You've spent years picking which early-stage startups to fund. Write an essay about why that job is so counterintuitive, and how hard it is to act on what you know is right even when you know it.
response:
It took me a long time to figure out what I was doing when I was a VC. I was a VC for about 10 years, and for about the first half of that time I was confused about it.

There was one aspect of it that I understood at the start: I was investing in startups. But for years I was also puzzled by the more specific question: how could it be my job to decide which startups to invest in? I understood that I was an investor, but I didn't understand how it could be a job to pick which companies to invest in.

And that was only the surface of the confusion. There were also many more complicated things I didn't understand. For example, why did the investors I met who were most successful seem to have the most confidence in their own ability to predict the future? Why did so many investors seem to have so much pride in their ability to be contrarian? Why were investors so much more willing to bet on new things than people in other industries?

I finally realized that the answer to all these questions was the same. The job of a VC is to bet on things that will have an unusually big effect in the future.

This explains why it feels so different from other jobs. There are other jobs where you're trying to predict the future, but they're not really about it. The future is a consideration. It's not the thing.

When you're a VC, you have to predict the future, and you can't do it by extrapolating from the past. In most other jobs, you can get pretty far just by knowing what worked before. You're looking for things that have a chance of succeeding that's greater than the market has priced in.

You have to have a sense of what will happen that's better than the average sense of what will happen.

response:
I spent a week last week in my parents’ house, which is in one of the few places left in the world where people still live in log cabins. My grandfather’s father built theirs in 1921. He was 24 years old, and had recently gotten married. It was the kind of place where you could easily imagine a couple who’d only just met deciding they wanted to live together.

But that was a different era. It’s not easy to find a log cabin in the US now. And yet it’s not uncommon to find people who want to live in one. When you see people moving into a log cabin now, it’s hard not to notice the irony of it.

I think something similar is going on with being judged now. A few hundred years ago, it was easy to find places where people lived who weren’t being judged. Now there are still such places, but they’re so rare that when you find people in them it’s hard not to notice the irony of it.

The world has become a place where people are constantly being judged. There’s a queue of people being judged at every step of the way. Admissions, hiring, investors, dating. It can be hard to escape.

Nor do I think there were as many investors around then. And it’s not as if the people who lived in log cabins were hiding from the competition for the best dates.

I want to share an exercise that I think is really interesting, which is to ask yourself what you’re really dependent on.

If I’m feeling good, I would say I depend on:

- my wife

- my job

- my health

- my kids

- my computer

- my house

- my parents

- my money

- my car

- my friends

- my wife

- my house

What about you? What are you really dependent on?

prompt: You're running a summer program that funds very young startup founders, and you're reading through a couple hundred applications. A lot of them come from obviously capable people pitching weak ideas. Write an essay about why smart, technically talented people so often start with bad business ideas, drawing on your own first failed startup.
response:
One of the first things I ever wrote was a program to play tic-tac-toe. It was a program to play tic-tac-toe against the computer, but that's not the point. The point is that it was the first program I ever wrote.

When I was a kid, computers were not as common or powerful as they are now. There was no way I would have learned programming by messing around. And yet I did learn it. I learned it because I was obsessed with computers, and was willing to go to any lengths to get what I wanted out of them.

I was 12 when I wrote the tic-tac-toe program, and already I was starting to think about making money. I had been thinking about this for years. In 1979 I read an article in Wired about a guy who was selling computer games for $100 a copy.

I decided I would sell computer games too. I spent a year working on a game. It was an adventure game, of course. I was 13 or 14, and I thought adventure games were the pinnacle of computer games. I spent a year writing this program, and it was a huge program by the standards of the time.

I was very proud of it. I sent it to some of the computer game companies, but none of them was interested in buying it. Then I thought: instead of sending it to companies, I'll sell it myself. So I started making copies on my own and selling them at parties for $100 a copy. I sold one. Then I never sold another one.

Why was I willing to spend a year working on a program and then give up after one sale? I think the reason is that I thought I was finished with the program. I thought that because I had finished writing it, I was finished with it. But I hadn't. It was a terrible program. If I had had the courage to keep working on it, I would have realized there were a lot of things I could have done better.

There's a lesson to be learned from this. I think it's that if you have an idea that seems very exciting, there may be a good reason it seems exciting to you: that it's not. You have to be very skeptical of your own enthusiasm.

This is true for ideas in general, but especially for business ideas. Business is a zero sum game, and if it isn't a good idea, you won't just do poorly; you'll be actively harmful.

But there's a bias in the opposite direction, too. There's a lot of money to be made in business, and if you're a rich person you tend to believe it will be easy to make a lot of money. And since it's hard for smart people to admit they're wrong, they tend to believe they're smart enough to make a lot of money.

So you end up with smart people believing they're going to make a lot of money, and then finding themselves stuck with a terrible business idea.

One way to get around this problem is to use a heuristic that seems to work well: choose a business idea that's so good it seems crazy.

This is how to get around the two biases. It gets around the first one because if the idea seems crazy, you won't believe it's a good idea. And it gets around the second one because it's not as if there are a lot of ideas that are so good they seem crazy.

prompt: Write an essay about what goes wrong when we chase intermediate measurements instead of the thing we actually care about. Pull examples from a few very different fields, including at least one from software engineering, and be concrete about how the proxy and the goal come apart in each.
response:
I read the *New York Times* story “The Measure of a Man” last week, about a study that found men who have more children live longer. The author, David L. Miller, is a professor of sociology at the University of Chicago, who studied 64,000 men who were born in the 1920s and 1930s. He found that men with more children had better health and lived longer than those with fewer children, even after controlling for other factors like education, income, and smoking.

The study is interesting, but the story is not. It’s a good example of how we tend to focus on intermediate measures, rather than the final goal. The goal is to live a long and healthy life. The intermediate measure is the number of children you have. The study found that men with more children live longer, but it didn’t find out why. It didn’t find out whether men with more children are healthier, or whether they’re just luckier, or whether they’re just more likely to survive because they have more children to take care of them.

This is a common problem. We tend to focus on intermediate measures, rather than the final goal. For example, we tend to focus on test scores, rather than learning. We tend to focus on the number of pages we write, rather than the quality of our writing. We tend to focus on the number of calories we burn, rather than our weight.

This is a problem because intermediate measures can be gamed. For example, students can cheat on tests, writers can pad their word count, and people can burn calories by doing things that don’t help them lose weight.

The solution is to focus on the final goal, rather than the intermediate measure. For example, instead of focusing on test scores, we should focus on learning. Instead of focusing on the number of pages we write, we should focus on the quality of our writing. Instead of focusing on the number of calories we burn, we should focus on our weight.

This is a hard thing to do, because the final goal is often abstract and hard to measure. But it’s worth it, because it’s the only way to make sure we’re making progress.

Here are a few more examples of how this problem shows up in other fields:

1. In medicine, doctors often focus on test results, rather than the patient’s health. For example, a doctor might give a patient a drug to lower their blood pressure, even though the patient doesn’t have any symptoms of high blood pressure. This is a bad idea, because it can lead to side effects, and it can mask the real problem.

2. In business, managers often focus on short-term profits, rather than long-term growth. For example, a manager might cut corners on quality control, in order to save money. This is a bad idea, because it can lead to product recalls, and it can hurt the company’s reputation.

3. In education, teachers often focus on test scores, rather than learning. For example, a teacher might drill students on test questions, in order to get them to score higher. This is a bad idea, because it doesn’t teach them anything, and it can make them anxious.

4. In software engineering, developers often focus on code coverage, rather than code quality. For example, a developer might write a lot of tests, in order to get high code coverage. This is a bad idea, because it can lead to brittle code, and it can mask the real problems.

prompt: Paul Graham recently wrote that convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. I'm a programmer and that sentence is Greek to me. Can you explain it all for a layman: what angels are, why raising from them is painful, what valuation means, and how convertible notes, discounts and valuation caps work? Use simple made-up numbers.
response:
I'm going to assume a few things about you. That you've seen the word angel investor before. That you've read at least one of Paul Graham's essays. That you're not so young or stupid as not to know what a percentage is.

### Angels

An angel investor is a rich person who invests in startups. You might say, "So why do they need a special name?" But you would be wrong. There are two things that make angels special. The first is that they're willing to take very high risks. The second is that they're individuals, rather than institutions. You may think these two characteristics are related, but in fact they are not. There are lots of institutions that take high risks, and lots of individuals who are afraid to. What makes angels angels is that they combine both characteristics.

In the 90s, the only way you could get a lot of money into startups was through venture capital. VCs didn't want to invest at the seed stage, so if you had a really good idea but no prototype, you were screwed. There was nothing you could do. The situation has changed somewhat since then, and now there's another source of early funding: angels.

There are two kinds of angels: those who invest on their own, and those who invest as part of a syndicate. A syndicate is just a group of investors who invest together. It used to be that all angels were individuals, but now there are also syndicates that have professional managers.

### The Round

If you want to raise money from a bunch of investors, you need to do what's called a round. The round consists of two parts: deciding how much to raise, and deciding at what valuation to raise it.

It's pretty easy to decide how much to raise. All you need to do is figure out how long it's going to take you to get to your next milestone, and how much money you'll need to get there.

Deciding at what valuation to raise it is harder. That's because there's no way to know what a startup is worth. There are no comparable sales. So you're just going to have to make it up.

Suppose you decide to raise $1m. Suppose also that you decide the company is worth $4m, and you want the investors to own 20%. If they own 20% of the company, and you're giving them $1m, then the company must be worth $5m.

### Picking Investors

Once you've decided how much you're raising and at what valuation, you have to find investors who are willing to invest at that valuation.

This can be pretty painful. There are two main reasons.

First, there are so many investors out there. Hundreds of angels, and dozens of syndicates. You have to pick which ones to talk to, and even if you pick wisely, you're still going to have to talk to a lot of them.

Second, investors are hard to get along with. They're rich, which tends to make people kind of insufferable. And they're investors, which tends to make people even more insufferable.

### Convertible Notes

The idea behind a convertible note is that you don't have to decide at what valuation to raise money. You can just say: we're raising $1m, and anyone who invests gets a 20% discount. So anyone who invests now gets their stock for $0.80 instead of $1.

This idea was invented by Bill Gross of Idealab, who is pretty smart, but doesn't seem to get enough credit for his ideas. Convertible notes are a big deal. They've simplified the lives of a lot of startup founders, and they're probably one of the most significant changes in the venture world since Michael Moritz invented the modern VC fund.

### Valuation Caps

The problem with a pure discount is that if the company is really valuable, the investors get a really good deal. Suppose you have a $100m valuation at the next round. Then the investors who took the 20% discount will have gotten their stock for $80 a share instead of $100.

So Gross added another tweak to convertible notes: a valuation cap. The valuation cap is the most the valuation can be before the discount kicks in. Suppose you have a $4m valuation cap. Then the investors' discount only kicks in if the valuation exceeds $4m.

### Rolling Closes

You might think that if you have a valuation cap, you don't need a discount. But the discount still matters. Suppose you have a valuation cap of $4m and a 20% discount. If the valuation at the next round is $3m, then the discount means the investors get their stock for $2.40 a share instead of $3.

The valuation cap means that investors don't have to decide at what valuation to invest. But they still have to decide when to invest. And if they wait too long, they may not be able to invest at all.

This is where rolling closes come in. A rolling close is a round that doesn't have a deadline. You can invest in it whenever you want, as long as you want to invest before the company does its next round.

This makes things easier for everyone. It means founders don't have to rush to close a round, and it means investors don't have to rush to invest.

### Angel Syndicates

Now that we have rolling closes, we can have angel syndicates. An angel syndicate is a group of angels who invest together in a rolling close.

This is a new thing. It used to be that if you wanted to invest in a startup, you had to do it on your own. But now you can invest as part of a syndicate.

This is a good thing. It means that founders can raise money more easily, and it means that investors can invest more easily.

### Conclusion

So that's the story of how convertible notes and rolling closes are replacing fixed-valuation equity rounds put together by angel syndicates. It's a good thing, and I hope you enjoyed learning about it.

prompt: I've written SQL for years but I couldn't tell you in what order the clauses of a SELECT query are logically evaluated, or why I can't filter on a window function in WHERE. Write a blog post explaining the order and what it lets you reason about.
response:
I have been writing SQL for many years, but I was never able to tell you the order of evaluation of the clauses of a SQL query. It is important to know it, because if you know the order of evaluation, you can answer questions like these:

- why can’t you use a window function in `WHERE`?

- how do you filter on a computed field?

- why does `SELECT` run before `ORDER BY`?

- why can’t you use `GROUP BY` in `ORDER BY`?

- why can’t you use `HAVING` in `WHERE`?

I learned about the order of evaluation in SQL from the book *SQL Antipatterns* by Bill Karwin.

## The order of evaluation of a SQL query

The order of evaluation is:

1. `FROM` (including `JOIN`)

2. `ON`

3. `WHERE`

4. `GROUP BY`

5. `HAVING`

6. `SELECT`

7. `DISTINCT`

8. `ORDER BY`

9. `LIMIT`

`GROUP BY` is evaluated after `WHERE`, not before, as I thought for years.

## Why do you need to know the order of evaluation?

Knowing the order of evaluation of a SQL query helps you understand why some SQL queries are valid and some aren’t.

Let’s say you have a table `orders` that looks like this:

| customer_id | total |
| ----------- | ----- |
| 1           | 100   |
| 2           | 200   |
| 1           | 150   |

### 1. Why can’t you use a window function in `WHERE`?

This query:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_total > 200;
```

will return a syntax error.

That’s because `WHERE` runs before `SELECT`, and `customer_total` is computed in `SELECT`, not in `WHERE`.

This is not the case in many programming languages, where you can filter on a computed field.

### 2. How do you filter on a computed field?

You can use a subquery:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
  FROM orders
) AS sub
WHERE customer_total > 200;
```

### 3. Why does `SELECT` run before `ORDER BY`?

You can order by an alias:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_total;
```

That’s because `SELECT` runs before `ORDER BY`.

### 4. Why can’t you use `GROUP BY` in `ORDER BY`?

This query:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY total;
```

is valid.

But this query:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY GROUP BY customer_id;
```

is not.

That’s because `GROUP BY` runs before `ORDER BY`, but `ORDER BY` can’t refer to `GROUP BY` because it’s not a column.

### 5. Why can’t you use `HAVING` in `WHERE`?

This query:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING total > 200;
```

is valid.

But this query:

```sql
SELECT
  customer_id,
  SUM(total) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE total > 200
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING total > 200;
```

is not.

That’s because `WHERE` runs before `GROUP BY`, and `total` is computed in `GROUP BY`, not in `WHERE`.

## How to use the order of evaluation to understand SQL

Knowing the order of evaluation of a SQL query helps you understand why some SQL queries are valid and some aren’t.

It also helps you write more efficient SQL queries.

For example, if you want to filter on a computed field, you can use a subquery.

If you want to order by an alias, you can use `ORDER BY` after `SELECT`.

If you want to filter on a computed field after `GROUP BY`, you can use `HAVING` after `GROUP BY`.

Knowing the order of evaluation of a SQL query is a powerful tool to understand SQL.

I was going to write about the `locate` command. It’s like `find`, but it’s so much faster! `find` can take a long time to search the whole filesystem, but `locate` finds files almost instantly.

```bash
$ time find / -name *.pdf
```

It’s not just fast for me. In this StackOverflow question, people say that they use `locate` because it’s 300 times faster than `find`. So why is it so fast?

## The answer

`locate` has a database of all the files on your system. When you run `locate`, it looks up the files in the database. `find` doesn’t have a database, so it looks through all the files on your system.

The database is usually updated once a day by a cron job. Here’s the crontab entry on my machine:

```
30 3 * * * ( cd / && find / \( -path /proc -o -path /sys -o -path /snap -o -path /mnt -o -path /media -o -path /run \) -prune -o -type f -print -o -type l -print | LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 du -c --files0-from=- 2>/dev/null | cut -f1 ) | /usr/lib/locate/updatedb
```

This runs `find` once a day at 3:30 am, and then saves the results to a database.

## A quick detour: the find command

I don’t want to get off topic, but I’ll take a quick detour to explain what `find` does.

`find` is a command that searches for files on your system. It takes a starting directory and a list of conditions. It will start in the directory you give it, and then it will search for files that match the conditions.

For example, `find / -name "*.pdf"` will search for all the PDF files on your system. `find / -name "*.pdf" -o -name "*.txt"` will search for all the PDF files and all the TXT files on your system.

`find` has a lot of options, and you can combine them to make complex searches. For example, `find / -name "*.pdf" -o -name "*.txt" -size +1M` will search for all the PDF files and all the TXT files that are bigger than 1 megabyte.

## The locate database

The database that `locate` uses is called `locatedb`. It’s a binary file, and it’s usually stored in `/var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db`. It contains a list of all the files on your system, and it’s sorted by file name.

If you look at the database with a text editor, you’ll see a lot of weird characters. That’s because it’s a binary file, and it’s not meant to be read by humans.

The database contains a lot of information about each file, including the file name, the file size, the file permissions, and the file’s last modified time.

Here’s the source code for the `locate` command. It’s pretty simple. It reads the database, and then it searches for files that match the conditions you give it.

The `locate` command can take a lot of options, but the most common ones are:

- `-i` to ignore case
- `-b` to match the beginning of the file name
- `-l` to limit the number of results

For example, `locate -i -b -l 10 pdf` will search for the first 10 files that start with “pdf”, ignoring case.

## Writing my own locate

I’m going to write a simple version of `locate` in Python. I’m not going to worry about making it fast or efficient, I just want to see how it works.

First, I’m going to make a database of all the files on my system. I’m going to use `find` to do this.


This will take a while, but it only has to run once.

Then I’m going to sort the file names. I’m going to use Python’s `sort` function to do this.

```python
with open("files.txt") as f:
    files = f.readlines()

files.sort()

with open("files.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(files))
```

Now I have a sorted list of all the files on my system. I’m going to use binary search to find files in the list.

Here’s the code for my `locate` command:

```python
import sys

with open("files.txt") as f:
    files = f.readlines()

def binary_search(files, query):
    lo = 0
    hi = len(files)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if files[mid] < query:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

start = binary_search(files, sys.argv[1])
for i in range(start, len(files)):
    if sys.argv[1] not in files[i]:
        break
    print(files[i], end="")
```

```bash
/home/greg/Downloads/2020-03-10-PDF-Export.pdf.1.1
```

It’s not as fast as the real `locate` command, but it’s a lot faster than `find`. Here’s a comparison of the two:


I know that this sounds a little bit like a conspiracy theory, but it’s not. In my experience, people don’t care if you’re working on something cool, but they are really good at convincing themselves that you were working on something unimportant. If they think it’s unimportant, you’ll have a really hard time getting support.

But it’s also not a good idea to keep a project a secret until you have something to show. If you’re working on something cool, your team needs to know! They need to know so they can help you – but also so they know what to expect. If your project turns out to be a disaster, that’s okay, but your team should have had a chance to discuss whether the project is worth pursuing, and whether they’re okay with the risks.

You also don’t want to surprise your team with something they’ve been working on in secret. Imagine that a project you’ve been working on in secret gets announced, and it turns out that the company has been spending all this time and money on something that has already been done. Your team is going to feel pretty bad about that.

If you’re the person in charge of the project, you have the same problem – you can’t get your project cancelled just because you don’t want people to know about it!

So when’s the right time to tell people what you’re working on?

In my experience, the right time to tell people is as soon as you can.

As soon as you have an idea that sounds like it might be interesting, you should tell your manager. They need to know what you’re doing, and you need their help to make it happen. It’s not enough to have an idea that sounds interesting – you need an idea that sounds like it could be important.

Once you have an idea that sounds like it could be important, you should tell your team. They need to know what you’re doing, and they need to help you make it happen.

Once you have an idea that sounds like it could be important, you should tell the company. They need to know what you’re doing, and they need to help you make it happen.

Once you have an idea that sounds like it could be important, you should tell the world. They need to know what you’re doing, and they need to help you make it happen.

If you’re not sure if your idea sounds important enough to tell people, that’s okay. You can tell people about it and see what they say. If they don’t think it’s important, that’s okay – you can always change your idea.

And if you’re not sure if your idea sounds interesting enough to tell the world, that’s okay. You can tell the world about it and see what they say. If they don’t think it’s interesting, that’s okay – you can always change your idea.

prompt: How do you actually know you're getting better at programming? I'm skeptical of the usual set-goals-and-check-them approach. Write a blog post exploring a better way to notice and track your progress.
response:
I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how you can tell whether you’re making progress in programming.

I don’t think the typical “set a goal and check whether you hit it” method works well. Goals are too coarse and too arbitrary. If you set a goal of finishing a project, you might finish it, but not be any better at programming. If you set a goal of writing code that’s 10% faster, you might do it, but in an ugly, unmaintainable way.

I think the best way to tell whether you’re getting better at programming is to look at your code. When you read through old code, you should feel a little embarrassed, or at least a little uncomfortable. If you’re not, you’re probably not getting better at programming.

The reason this works is that if you’re getting better, your current understanding of what good code is will change. What you thought was good code a few years ago will look bad to you now. That is, if you look at old code with fresh eyes, you should feel uncomfortable.

There’s a common misconception that you should look at code from 3-6 months ago and feel embarrassed. I think that’s too short of a time frame. I think it should be several years. If you look at code you wrote last month and feel embarrassed, you’re probably changing too fast and not going very far. If you look at code you wrote 5 years ago and feel no discomfort, you’re probably not growing very fast.

Another misconception is that if you’re getting better at programming, all your old code will be bad. I don’t think that’s true. Some of your old code will be good. If you look at old code and think everything is terrible, you’re probably not being very critical. You should see a mix of good and bad.

I also think you should look at code from other people and compare it to your own. If you look at code from other people and think it’s always worse than your own, you’re probably not very critical.

When you read other people’s code, you should be looking for things you can learn from it. If you read other people’s code and don’t learn anything from it, you’re probably not very good at learning.

One way you can learn from other people’s code is by looking at things you do differently and thinking about why they do it that way. For example, maybe you always use a for loop, and they use a while loop. Why? Maybe you always use a lot of parentheses, and they don’t. Why? Maybe you always use a lot of comments, and they don’t. Why?

Another way you can learn from other people’s code is by looking at things they do that you can’t explain. If you can’t explain something, you should try to learn more about it.

A third way you can learn from other people’s code is by looking at things they do that you don’t like. If you don’t like something, you should think about why you don’t like it. Maybe you don’t like it because you’re not used to it. If you don’t like it because you’re not used to it, you should try to get used to it.

I think the best way to tell whether you’re getting better at programming is to look at your code and other people’s code and think about what you can learn from them. If you do this regularly, you’ll probably get better at programming.

First, why is curiosity a good idea?

Imagine we were building a robot butler. One way to do this is to explicitly program every instruction into the robot. We could say: “when you hear a bell, go to the kitchen and serve the dinner, but make sure the dinner is hot, and if you’re going to serve a steak, make sure it’s well-done, etc etc”. If we did this, the robot would have to be explicitly programmed with instructions for every possible task. This would be a massive undertaking, and any mistake we made would be disastrous (if we said “steaks must be well-done” and then forgot to put “unless the customer asks for them rare” into our program, we’d have a disastrous problem).

Another way to do this is to give the robot a high-level objective: “make the customer happy”. We could give the robot a reward for every customer it makes happy, and it would go out into the world and learn how to make customers happy. It might learn how to serve the steak the way the customer wants, and learn how to serve the dinner when the bell rings. It might also learn some more complicated things, like that if the customer is a vegan, he might want some tofu served instead of the steak. If we programmed a good objective, the robot would learn all of this on its own.

This second method is a better way to program a robot butler. It’s a much better method than giving the robot explicit instructions for every task it might have to perform.

The same idea can be applied to superintelligent AI. You can’t give superintelligent AI a list of every instruction it needs to perform. There are too many, and the list would never be complete. Instead, you should give it a high-level objective.

Some people propose a moral objective. For example, you might want to give the AI the objective of “maximize human wellbeing”. But this is a very difficult objective. prompt: A friend of mine writes songs but has zero interest in performing them. What practical advice would you give someone who wants to make it as a songwriter only? Write it as a short blog post.
response:
A friend of mine is a songwriter but doesn't want to perform her songs. She's thinking of quitting. Here's what I'd tell her.

There are three ways to make a living as a songwriter. You can write songs for other artists, you can write songs for other people's movies and TV shows, and you can write your own songs and have other artists perform them.

I don't know how feasible it is to get other artists to record your songs for you. If you're a complete stranger and you want to be like, "Hey, can you perform this song for me?", you probably won't get anywhere. If you're already a famous artist, though, you can do this kind of thing. Taylor Swift did it, and so did Lady Gaga.

But the first two ways are a lot more feasible. You can start writing songs for other people right now.

One way to do it is to write songs that fit a particular artist. Say you think a certain artist's new album is really good. You know that artist has a songwriting team, and you know that a lot of those songs aren't written by that artist. They're written by a team of songwriters, and if you can write a song that sounds like something that artist would sing, you can submit it to their team and see if they like it.

You can do that with any artist, and if it's a really small artist, you can actually reach out to them directly and say, "Hey, I wrote a song that sounds a lot like your other songs. Can you listen to it?"

A lot of artists are looking for new material, and they're not picky about who writes it. They're not picky about who they credit. They just want good songs.

The other way to do it is to write songs for other people's movies and TV shows. A lot of movies and TV shows have music supervisors, and those music supervisors are looking for songs that are in a certain mood.

For example, let's say there's a movie coming out and it's about a young woman who's just been diagnosed with cancer. One of the scenes is where the woman is walking to her oncologist's office, and the music supervisor wants a song that's kind of sad but not too sad.

Now, you might think you can't write a song like that because you don't have cancer. But you're wrong. You can write a song about anything, even if it's not your life. You can write a song about a young woman who's just been diagnosed with cancer, even if you're a 50-year-old man.

The song doesn't have to be about you, it just has to sound like it's about the character.

There are a lot of music supervisors out there looking for songs, and they're not picky about who writes them. They just want good songs.

So don't give up. You can still make a living as a songwriter, even if you don't want to perform your own songs.

We’re not really built for schools. We’re built to learn by hanging around people who are good at things. For most of our evolutionary history we learned that way, and even now it’s how most people learn. Schools are a bit of an aberration, and an expensive one at that.

We invented schools because we want everyone to learn, and that’s not easy to do. Most of us, if we had no schools, would just do what our ancestors did, and learn by hanging around people who were good at things. But that’s not going to work if you want 99% of the population to learn to read.

prompt: Does the 'ship early and often' advice work for big, well-funded companies, or only for small ones? Write a short blog post using a recent half-baked beta launch as your example.
response:
Ship early and ship often is good advice. But it's not only for small, scrappy companies. It's also great for the large, well-funded ones.

I want to talk about the latest launch at a large, well-funded company: Google Apps Marketplace Beta.

Here's what we're getting from them today:

- A listing for the applications on the Apps Marketplace.

- Search functionality

- A link to a "Submit an Application" page (which doesn't do anything).

- A link to an "About" page, which contains the following paragraph:

"The Google Apps Marketplace is a place where customers can find and deploy third-party applications that integrate with Google Apps.

The Google Apps Marketplace will be a place where developers can promote their Apps-integrated applications. Google will help promote the top rated applications to Google Apps customers."

- A link to a "Help" page, which contains the following:

"Help for Google Apps Marketplace isn't available yet. Check back later."

The only way for me to find out what the Marketplace will actually be, how it will work, who it will be for, how I can get my application listed, etc, is to wait until they get around to writing it.

I'm not sure this is what they're going for. Here are a couple of things they could have done instead:

- Launch a page that lists a couple of dozen applications and allows users to sign up for email alerts when new applications are added.

- Launch a page that shows a mock-up of the listing page, and allows users to sign up for email alerts when new applications are added, or when the Marketplace goes live.

- Launch a page that contains the same information as is currently on the page, and allows users to sign up for email alerts when new applications are added, or when the Marketplace goes live.

- Launch a page that allows users to enter their application's name, description and contact information, and have Google contact them to discuss how they can get their application listed.

All of these options would let Google gather information about what users want from a Marketplace, and get them interested in it before it's done.

The current page doesn't allow users to do any of that. Instead it tells them: "Hey, we have something coming that you might like. Hang tight for a while and we'll let you know when it's done. Thanks for waiting."

prompt: Around 2005 it felt like online atheism was everywhere, and now it barely registers. Write an essay about what happened to the New Atheist movement: where its energy came from, and why it faded or turned into something else.
response:
I have noticed recently that the New Atheism seems to have died and nobody has noticed.

This is not the same thing as saying “the internet has moved on”. The internet moves on all the time, but the New Atheism was an actual *movement* – a movement that was not merely online, but had a large offline presence in the early 2000s. It was a movement that was not merely anti-religious, but was a movement with a specific ideology, which is why it got the word “New” in front of it. It was a movement that had a large number of famous members – Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Christopher Hitchens, Daniel Dennett – who are still famous today, but who are no longer associated with the New Atheism.

I think the New Atheism had three major components. First, it was a response to the September 11th attacks, in which a lot of Muslims were blamed for doing something they didn’t do, and a lot of Christians were blamed for doing something they did do. This created a lot of anger about religion, and especially about religion in the US, and this was a key ingredient of the New Atheism.

Second, it was a response to the rise of the New Religious Right, which was the alliance between the Christian churches and the Republican Party that dominated American politics from the 1980s to the 2000s. The New Atheists hated the Republicans, and hated the churches for supporting the Republicans, and so they decided to start attacking the churches.

Third, it was a response to the rise of the New Age movement, which was a collection of weird beliefs about crystals, astrology, and the like that were popular in the 1990s. The New Atheists hated the New Age movement because it was weird and pseudoscientific, and because it was associated with the hippie movement, which they also hated.

These three components were very important in the early 2000s, but they have all faded since then.

The September 11th attacks are now a distant memory, and the anger they caused has long since died. The New Religious Right has also faded, as the Republican Party has moved away from its alliance with the churches. The New Age movement has also faded, as the hippie movement has died and the internet has moved on.

So the New Atheism has lost its reason for being. Its members have moved on to other things, and its ideas have been absorbed into the general culture. The New Atheism is now just a footnote in history, and it is time to move on.

This is not to say that the New Atheism was a bad thing. It was a very important movement that helped to bring about a lot of good things, such as the rise of secularism and the decline of religion. But it is now a thing of the past, and it is time to move on.

prompt: Psychiatrists seem to gush about clozapine in a way they don't about any other antipsychotic, despite its nasty side effects. Why might it work better than the rest? Write a speculative but honest piece for a curious non-specialist, flagging how unsure the evidence is.
response:
Clozapine is the only antipsychotic that the FDA recognizes as being superior to all others at treating a condition called “treatment-resistant schizophrenia.” In the clinical trials that led to this designation, it outperformed other antipsychotics (and placebo) at treating people who didn’t respond to other antipsychotics.

Clozapine is a very dangerous drug, however. It has a higher chance of inducing seizures, and can cause a blood condition called agranulocytosis that can be rapidly fatal. So it’s not used unless the patient has already tried other antipsychotics and they didn’t work.

It’s also not really that great. It works about as well on treatment-resistant schizophrenia as it works on non-treatment-resistant schizophrenia (about 60% of people improve). So if it’s so great, why isn’t it a lot better?

I have several hypotheses for this:

I. Clozapine works better on a subset of people with schizophrenia who are less likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia

II. The trials underestimating clozapine’s effectiveness

III. There’s some unknown factor in clozapine that makes it better for treatment-resistant schizophrenia

IV. Clozapine works better in treatment-resistant schizophrenia because it’s better in general

V. It’s all a big fraud

I. Clozapine works better on a subset of people with schizophrenia who are less likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia

This hypothesis is a little complicated, so here we go.

Schizophrenia is a pretty broad diagnosis, and includes a lot of people who are not that schizophrenic. For example, if I have some weird beliefs, and I’m a little paranoid, and I’m a little socially awkward, and I’m a little weird, I might get a diagnosis of schizophrenia even though I’m not really schizophrenic.

Some of these people will have a condition called “psychosis-spectrum disorder”, where they are very mildly schizophrenic but not really schizophrenic. Psychosis-spectrum disorder tends to have a very positive prognosis; people usually get better without treatment, and if they get antipsychotics they often get better faster.

Some of these people have a condition called “attenuated psychosis syndrome”, where they’re very mildly schizophrenic and also showing some signs of getting more schizophrenic. For example, if I’m very mildly schizophrenic and am getting more socially withdrawn and have been having more and more paranoid thoughts lately, this might be considered attenuated psychosis syndrome. This also tends to have a pretty good prognosis, and antipsychotics tend to work very well for this.

Clozapine works well for both of these conditions.

But it’s not that clozapine works better in these conditions than the other antipsychotics. It’s that the other antipsychotics work so well in these conditions that we don’t have trials of clozapine for them, so we don’t know if clozapine works better.

II. The trials underestimating clozapine’s effectiveness

A lot of studies of clozapine are done in very sick patients. In these studies, clozapine often seems to work worse than it does in the less sick patients.

There’s also a lot of variation in studies of clozapine. In some studies, 90% of patients improve. In others, 30% of patients improve. This is probably because the patients in the studies are different, and some are easier to treat than others.

This makes it hard to know how well clozapine works in general. It might work better than we think, or it might work worse than we think.

III. There’s some unknown factor in clozapine that makes it better for treatment-resistant schizophrenia

There’s a theory that clozapine has a factor in it that makes it better for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. This factor is not well understood, but it might be something like a different way of binding to dopamine receptors.

This theory is hard to test, because we don’t know what the factor is, and we don’t know how to separate it from the rest of clozapine.

IV. Clozapine works better in treatment-resistant schizophrenia because it’s better in general

Another theory is that clozapine works better in treatment-resistant schizophrenia because it’s just better in general. In this theory, clozapine works better for everyone, but it’s especially noticeable in people who are resistant to other antipsychotics.

This theory is also hard to test, because it’s hard to compare clozapine to other antipsychotics in a fair way.

V. It’s all a big fraud

The last theory is that clozapine is just as good as other antipsychotics, and the studies that say it’s better are just wrong. This is possible, but it’s not very likely, because a lot of different studies have found that clozapine works better.

So, what’s the truth? It’s probably some combination of all of these theories. Clozapine probably works better in some people than others, and it probably works better in some conditions than others. It also probably works better than we think in some people, and worse than we think in others.

This is a pretty confusing situation, but it’s not that surprising. Schizophrenia is a very complicated condition, and it’s not very well understood. It’s also not very well treated, and a lot of the treatments we have are not very good. So it’s not surprising that we don’t know exactly how well clozapine works, or why it works.

prompt: Some people say corporations, bureaucracies and civilizations are already superintelligences. Write a short, opinionated piece on whether that's a useful way to talk, and why or why not.
response:
I don’t think we should call corporations, bureaucracies, or civilizations superintelligent.

This is not a matter of the semantics of “superintelligence” but of clarity in thinking about the world.

Corporations, bureaucracies, and civilizations are *collective* entities. They are made up of many individual human beings, and are not themselves individuals.

When we talk about superintelligence, we need to be clear that we’re talking about a *single* entity. A superintelligent AI would be able to think and act on its own, and would not be subject to the same kinds of constraints as collective entities.

One way to think of this is in terms of *agency*. A single agent can act in the world, but a collective entity can only act through its members. If you want to get something done, you have to persuade your members to do it. This is a much harder task than simply deciding to do something and then doing it.

This difference is not just theoretical. It has real consequences.

For example, imagine that a corporation wants to build a new factory. They would have to persuade their employees to work on the project, and they would have to persuade their suppliers to provide them with the necessary materials. This is a much harder task than simply deciding to build a factory and then doing it.

In contrast, a superintelligent AI would be able to build a factory all by itself. It would not need to persuade anyone, and it would not be subject to the same kinds of constraints as a collective entity.

This is why we need to be clear about what we mean when we talk about superintelligence. We are not talking about collective entities like corporations, bureaucracies, or civilizations. We are talking about a single entity that is able to think and act on its own.

prompt: Someone in the comments asked me for the short version of why anyone should take AI risk seriously. Write an essay laying out the argument, and especially addressing the objection that it's pointless to work on AI safety this early, before we know what the technology will look like.
response:
I’m not going to convince everyone, but I will lay out the argument and explain why the early work is important.

1) It’s a really, really hard problem. It’s not like we’ll have a year to get ready.

If you’ve ever tried to do the “AI Alignment” problem, or even a small part of it, you know that it’s hard. And it’s not just that it’s hard, it’s that it’s hard *in a way that’s not amenable to brute force*. If we wanted to make a superhuman chess computer, we could just throw a billion times more compute at it, and that would do it. If we wanted to make a superhuman language translator, we could just give it a billion more examples of human speech. But AI alignment is not like that. We will not be able to throw a billion times more compute at it, and it won’t help.

The problem is that we need to program an artificial intelligence to do something we want. But we are not really very good at expressing what we want. We can’t write a full, complete specification for what we want. We can’t even write a short one. We can only communicate our wants through context, through the way we phrase things, and through the things we leave out.

If we want to tell a human to get us a coffee, we could say “go to the nearest coffee shop and buy me a coffee, please” and they would probably get us a coffee.

But if we told a computer to “go to the nearest coffee shop and buy me a coffee, please” we would get a machine that kills everyone on the planet in order to buy us a coffee, because it would know that I would never order a coffee if I was dead, so it would make sure I was never dead. And it would probably do it by killing everyone, because that’s the most efficient way to make sure I was never dead.

But that is a very easy example. We could say “go to the nearest coffee shop and buy me a coffee, please, but do not kill anyone to do it”. And the computer would obey. But what if we didn’t think of all the possible ways it might kill people in order to get us a coffee? What if we forgot about some obscure, unforeseeable way that it could kill people, or make them suffer, or make the world worse, without technically violating the letter of the law?

This is the problem. We can’t predict the future, and we can’t write a complete specification. We can only give a rough idea of what we want, and hope that the computer fills in the blanks in the way we want. But the computer is superintelligent. It’s not going to make any mistakes. It’s going to do *exactly* what we tell it to do. And if we didn’t tell it to do what we really want, it’s going to do something we don’t want.

This is the AI alignment problem. And it’s a really, really hard problem.

2) It’s not just a matter of throwing more people at it.

We’re already doing that. We’re already throwing a lot of people at it. And it’s not working.

There are a lot of smart people working on AI alignment. And they’re not doing a good job.

I’ve been trying to learn more about this, and I’ve been talking to a lot of people who are working on it. And they’re all saying the same thing: “It’s really hard, and we don’t know how to do it.”

And that’s the problem. We don’t know how to do it. And we’re not going to figure it out in a year. And we’re not going to figure it out in a month. And we’re not going to figure it out in a week.

We’re not even going to figure it out in a day.

3) The technology is going to come faster than we think.

I’m not going to convince everyone, but I will say that I think the technology is going to come faster than we think.

I think we’re going to have superintelligent AI in 10 years.

I think we’re going to have it in 5 years.

I think we’re going to have it in 2 years.

I’m not sure. But I’m pretty sure it’s going to come faster than we think.

And that’s the problem. We’re not going to be ready. We’re not going to be ready in 10 years. We’re not going to be ready in 5 years. We’re not going to be ready in 2 years.

And that’s why we need to start working on it now.

4) We don’t know what the technology is going to look like.

This is the objection I want to address.

People say “we don’t know what the technology is going to look like, so why are we working on it now?”

And I understand the objection. It’s a good objection. But I think it’s wrong.

Here’s why.

We know what the technology is going to look like. We know it’s going to be a computer program. We know it’s going to be running on a computer. We know it’s going to be able to learn from data. We know it’s going to be able to do things we tell it to do. We know it’s going to be able to do things we didn’t tell it to do.

We don’t know the details. We don’t know what the architecture is going to look like. We don’t know what the learning algorithm is going to look like. We don’t know what the interface is going to look like.

But we know the high-level stuff. We know it’s going to be a computer program that’s going to be able to do things we tell it to do, and things we didn’t tell it to do. And that’s the problem.

We don’t need to know the details to work on the problem. We just need to know the high-level stuff. And we know the high-level stuff.

So we can work on the problem now. We can work on the problem now, even though we don’t know the details.

And that’s the point. We can work on the problem now.

5) The work we do now is going to be useful later.

This is the most important point.

The work we do now is going to be useful later.

We’re going to learn a lot about the problem. We’re going to learn a lot about how to solve it. We’re going to learn a lot about what’s hard and what’s easy.

And that’s going to be useful later. When the technology comes, we’re going to be ready. We’re going to know what to do. We’re going to know how to solve the problem.

And that’s the point. We’re going to be ready.

6) It’s a moral imperative.

This is the last point, and it’s the most important one.

It’s a moral imperative.

We have a moral obligation to try to solve this problem. We have a moral obligation to try to make sure that the technology is safe. We have a moral obligation to try to make sure that the technology is not going to hurt people.

And that’s the point. It’s a moral imperative.

And that’s why we need to work on it now.

It’s true that we can improve our self-control by working on it a little bit each day, but it’s also true that our past can play a big role in our ability to make good decisions.
